author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
You can only fight magic with magic. 

Stop reviewing code generated by AI manually, you can't keep up.  It is better to implement an AI code review system to catch stupid vibe coding mistakes, at least most of them, only flag human review on hard cases

author.name: Mariusz Przygodzki
author.headline: Seasoned Sales Director | Public Sector | 💠 Embedded Software Engineer (OSS, C++/Rust)

comments.text: If AI-generated code requires systematic review by another AI, that's a signal your software development process is fundamentally flawed. Instead of fixing the root cause, you're proposing to add another layer of automation that will likely introduce its own errors and blind spots. Code review isn't just about catching bugs. It's about knowledge transfer, architectural discussions, establishing team standards, and mentoring. Automating this process robs the team of one of its most important moments of collaboration and learning.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: Mariusz Przygodzki there are some problems that are a lot easier to catch with rule based checks than praying the AI won't suddenly go stupid in the generation.

author.name: Mariusz Przygodzki
author.headline: Seasoned Sales Director | Public Sector | 💠 Embedded Software Engineer (OSS, C++/Rust)

replies.text:
Horace Chan Exactly. Rule-based checks (linters, static analysis, type checkers) are deterministic and transparent. You know exactly what they're checking and why. They catch the same issues consistently, every single time.
Using AI to review AI-generated code means you're stacking probabilistic systems on top of each other. Both can hallucinate, miss context, or make inconsistent decisions. You end up with compounding uncertainty instead of reliable guardrails.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: Mariusz Przygodzki Oh.  I mean using AI to create rule-base checks ahead of time, not running LLM live to check the output of another LLM.

comments.text: Two of the most important aspects of code review are: (1) how do the changes fit in the architecture and maintainability of the code base? and (2) what new insights into our code architecture and strategic planning can we gain from the new code and the context of the code change? Can we make this a responsibility of the AI agent in its review mode? How would new findings and an evolving architectural roadmap be communicated to the team? I think you are suggesting that we can flag certain PRs as important for human review, but in my experience some of my best insights have come from reviewing simple PRs that might otherwise just be rubber stamped. We may want to consider how AI can expose and communicate strategic insights during code review.

author.name: Aryan Lohia
author.headline: Automating Indian Businesses with AI | COO @ AI Hive | Helping professionals & founders use AI in their work, 1:1 | DM “AI”

comments.text:
I agree with the direction, but the implementation matters. An AI reviewer trained only on generic best practices will miss context-specific failures.

The teams getting value are the ones grounding AI review in their own production incidents, style guides, and failure modes. Otherwise you just automate confidence, not correctness.

author.name: Waqar Ali
author.headline: Full Stack Engineer for AI & SaaS (React, Next.js, Laravel) - Voice & Workflow Automation

comments.text: The tricky part is defining “hard cases.” AI doesn’t always know what it doesn’t know. But yeah, using AI as a first pass filter beats drowning in PRs you’ll never get to anyway.

author.name: Sacha Sindorf
author.headline: Artificial Intelligence Developer | Computer Vision, Coq, software verification, formal methods

comments.text:
Developers and testers lose contact with the design. You get contect by engaging with the design. Which they do less, because AI does it.

Then they don't know in depth what it does, what it is supposed to do, what it is not supposed to do. Reviewing hard cases is bound to get more challenging. People cannot reach there anymore.

This is the scenario we want to avoid.
